solution:
**Data:** \(\nu = 5 \times 10^{14}\) Hz. Planck's constant \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s (the value used throughout this chapter).

The energy carried by a single photon of radiation of frequency \(\nu\) is

\(E = h\nu\)

\(\therefore\ E = (6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}) \times (5 \times 10^{14}\ \text{s}^{-1})\)

\(\therefore\ E = 3.315 \times 10^{-19}\) J

Expressed in electronvolt, dividing by \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C,

\(E = \dfrac{3.315 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.072\) eV

Note that the light is monochromatic, so every photon in the beam carries exactly this same energy; making the beam brighter increases the NUMBER of photons per second, not the energy of each one.

**Answer: each photon carries \(E = 3.315 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 2.072\) eV.**

**Data:** slope of the \(V_0\) versus \(\nu\) graph \(= 4.1 \times 10^{-15}\) V s, \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C.

Einstein's photoelectric equation gives the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons as \(K_{max} = h\nu - \phi\). At the stopping potential \(V_0\) the most energetic electron is just turned back, so \(eV_0 = K_{max}\), giving

\(eV_0 = h\nu - \phi\)

\(\therefore\ V_0 = \left(\dfrac{h}{e}\right)\nu - \dfrac{\phi}{e}\)

This is a straight line in \(V_0\) against \(\nu\), and its **slope is \(h/e\)** — a slope that is the same for every emitter material, which is exactly why this experiment measures \(h\).

\(\therefore\ h = \text{slope} \times e = (4.1 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{V s}) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C})\)

\(\therefore\ h = 6.56 \times 10^{-34}\) J s

This is within about 1% of the accepted value \(6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s, consistent with the slope being quoted as approximate.

**Answer: \(h = 6.56 \times 10^{-34}\) J s.**

**Data:** threshold wavelength of tungsten \(\lambda_0 = 2.76 \times 10^{-5}\) cm \(= 2.76 \times 10^{-7}\) m. Take \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s, \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s, \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C.

**(a) Why no emission beyond the threshold wavelength**

The work function is the energy of a photon at the threshold:

\(\phi_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{2.76 \times 10^{-7}} = 7.207 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 4.504\) eV

A photon's energy \(E = hc/\lambda\) is **inversely** proportional to its wavelength. So if \(\lambda > \lambda_0\), then \(E < \phi_0\): a single photon simply does not carry enough energy to free an electron from the tungsten surface. Since one electron absorbs one whole photon, and it cannot accumulate energy from several photons, no electron is emitted no matter how intense the beam is or how long it is left on. Increasing the intensity only sends more of these too-weak photons per second.

**(b)(i) Ultraviolet radiation of \(\lambda = 1.80 \times 10^{-5}\) cm \(= 1.80 \times 10^{-7}\) m**

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{1.80 \times 10^{-7}} = 1.105 \times 10^{-18}\) J \(= 6.906\) eV

By Einstein's equation,

\(K_{max} = E - \phi_0 = 1.105 \times 10^{-18} - 7.207 \times 10^{-19}\)

\(\therefore\ K_{max} = 3.843 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 2.402\) eV

**(b)(ii) Radiation of frequency \(\nu = 4 \times 10^{15}\) Hz**

\(E = h\nu = (6.63 \times 10^{-34})(4 \times 10^{15}) = 2.652 \times 10^{-18}\) J \(= 16.575\) eV

\(K_{max} = E - \phi_0 = 2.652 \times 10^{-18} - 7.207 \times 10^{-19}\)

\(\therefore\ K_{max} = 1.931 \times 10^{-18}\) J \(= 12.07\) eV

Both incident radiations lie above the threshold (their frequencies exceed \(\nu_0 = c/\lambda_0 = 1.087 \times 10^{15}\) Hz), so emission does occur in each case.

**Answer: (a) because \(\lambda > \lambda_0\) makes the photon energy less than the work function \(\phi_0 = 4.504\) eV, and an electron cannot pool energy from several photons. (b)(i) \(K_{max} = 3.843 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 2.402\) eV; (ii) \(K_{max} = 1.931 \times 10^{-18}\) J \(= 12.07\) eV.**

**Data:** \(\lambda_1 = 4950\ \mathring{A} = 4950 \times 10^{-10}\) m with stopping potential \(V_{01} = 0.8\) V; second source has \(V_{02} = 1.2\) V. Take \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s, \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s, \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C.

The photocurrent vanishes when the retarding potential just stops the most energetic electron, so that retarding potential IS the stopping potential. Einstein's equation gives

\(eV_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi\)

**Work function of the cathode**

Energy of a photon from the first source:

\(E_1 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{4950 \times 10^{-10}} = 4.018 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 2.511\) eV

\(\therefore\ \phi = E_1 - eV_{01} = 2.511 - 0.8 = 1.711\) eV

\(\therefore\ \phi = 1.711 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 2.738 \times 10^{-19}\) J

The work function is a property of the cathode material, so it is unchanged when the source is swapped.

**Wavelength of the second source**

\(E_2 = \phi + eV_{02} = 1.711 + 1.2 = 2.911\) eV \(= 4.658 \times 10^{-19}\) J

\(\therefore\ \lambda_2 = \dfrac{hc}{E_2} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{4.658 \times 10^{-19}} = 4.270 \times 10^{-7}\) m

\(\therefore\ \lambda_2 = 4270\ \mathring{A}\)

The second stopping potential is larger, so the second source must be the more energetic one — and indeed its wavelength is **shorter** than 4950 \(\mathring{A}\), which is the consistency check on the answer.

**Answer: \(\phi = 1.711\) eV \(= 2.738 \times 10^{-19}\) J and \(\lambda_2 = 4270\ \mathring{A} = 4.270 \times 10^{-7}\) m.**

**Data:** \(\lambda = 4500\ \mathring{A} = 4500 \times 10^{-10}\) m, work function \(\phi = 2.0\) eV, radius of the circular path \(r = 20\) cm \(= 0.20\) m. Take \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s, \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s, \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C, \(m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\) kg.

**Step 1 — energy of the incident photon**

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{4500 \times 10^{-10}} = 4.42 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 2.7625\) eV

**Step 2 — kinetic energy of the most energetic photoelectron**

\(K_{max} = E - \phi = 2.7625 - 2.0 = 0.7625\) eV

\(\therefore\ K_{max} = 0.7625 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 1.22 \times 10^{-19}\) J

**Step 3 — its speed and momentum**

\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K_{max}}{m_e}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.22 \times 10^{-19}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}} = 5.175 \times 10^{5}\) m/s

\(p = m_e v = (9.11 \times 10^{-31})(5.175 \times 10^{5}) = 4.715 \times 10^{-25}\) kg m/s

**Step 4 — the magnetic field**

An electron entering perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\) experiences a force \(evB\) always at right angles to its velocity, which supplies the centripetal force:

\(evB = \dfrac{m_e v^{2}}{r}\qquad \therefore\ r = \dfrac{m_e v}{eB} = \dfrac{p}{eB}\)

\(\therefore\ B = \dfrac{p}{er} = \dfrac{4.715 \times 10^{-25}}{(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(0.20)}\)

\(\therefore\ B = 1.473 \times 10^{-5}\) T

(The most energetic electrons trace the LARGEST circle, so this field is the one that fits the observed radius of 20 cm.)

**Answer: \(B = 1.473 \times 10^{-5}\) T \(\approx 1.47 \times 10^{-5}\) T.**

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(\nu_0 = 6.761 \times 10^{14}\) Hz and \(\lambda_0 = 4438\ \mathring{A}\), and both are inconsistent with the key's OWN \(h\) and \(\phi\). The threshold frequency is fixed by \(\nu_0 = \phi/h\); with the key's own \(\phi = 2.801\) eV \(= 4.482 \times 10^{-19}\) J and \(h = 6.427 \times 10^{-34}\) J s that is \(6.973 \times 10^{14}\) Hz, whence \(\lambda_0 = c/\nu_0 = 4302\ \mathring{A}\). Run backwards, the printed \(6.761 \times 10^{14}\) Hz would require \(\phi = 2.716\) eV, which the same key does not print. The error propagates into \(\lambda_0\), since \(4438\ \mathring{A}\) is exactly \(c\) divided by the wrong frequency. The key's \(h\) and \(\phi\) agree with our derivation.]

**Data:** \((\lambda_1, V_{01}) = (2536\ \mathring{A},\ 1.95\ \text{V})\) and \((\lambda_2, V_{02}) = (3650\ \mathring{A},\ 0.5\ \text{V})\). Take \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s and \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C (\(h\) is what we are asked to find, so it must not be assumed).

Einstein's equation for each observation:

\(eV_{01} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_1} - \phi \qquad \text{and} \qquad eV_{02} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - \phi\)

**Step 1 — eliminate \(\phi\) to get \(h\)**

Subtracting the second from the first removes the unknown work function:

\(e(V_{01} - V_{02}) = hc\left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_1} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_2}\right)\)

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{1}{2536 \times 10^{-10}} = 3.943 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), \(\quad \dfrac{1}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{1}{3650 \times 10^{-10}} = 2.740 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}\)

\(\therefore\ \dfrac{1}{\lambda_1} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_2} = 1.2035 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}\)

\(e(V_{01} - V_{02}) = (1.6 \times 10^{-19})(1.95 - 0.5) = 2.32 \times 10^{-19}\) J

\(\therefore\ hc = \dfrac{2.32 \times 10^{-19}}{1.2035 \times 10^{6}} = 1.928 \times 10^{-25}\) J m

\(\therefore\ h = \dfrac{1.928 \times 10^{-25}}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 6.426 \times 10^{-34}\) J s

**Step 2 — the work function**

\(\phi = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_1} - eV_{01} = (1.928 \times 10^{-25})(3.943 \times 10^{6}) - 3.12 \times 10^{-19}\)

\(\therefore\ \phi = 7.601 \times 10^{-19} - 3.12 \times 10^{-19} = 4.481 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 2.80\) eV

(Using the second data point instead gives the same \(4.481 \times 10^{-19}\) J, as it must.)

**Step 3 — threshold frequency and wavelength**

\(\nu_0 = \dfrac{\phi}{h} = \dfrac{4.481 \times 10^{-19}}{6.426 \times 10^{-34}} = 6.974 \times 10^{14}\) Hz

\(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{c}{\nu_0} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{6.974 \times 10^{14}} = 4.302 \times 10^{-7}\) m \(= 4302\ \mathring{A}\)

**Step 4 — the emitter material**

Comparing \(\phi = 2.80\) eV with Table 14.1 (Potassium 2.3, Sodium 2.4, **Calcium 2.9**, Zinc 3.6 eV), the closest value is that of **calcium**.

**Answer: \(h = 6.43 \times 10^{-34}\) J s, \(\phi = 4.481 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 2.80\) eV, \(\nu_0 = 6.97 \times 10^{14}\) Hz, \(\lambda_0 = 4302\ \mathring{A}\); the emitter is most likely calcium.**

**Data:** (a) accelerating potential \(V = 54\) V; (b) kinetic energy \(= 150\) eV. Take \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s, \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C, \(m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\) kg.

For a particle of kinetic energy \(K\), the momentum is \(p = \sqrt{2mK}\), the de Broglie wavelength is \(\lambda = h/p\), and the speed is \(v = p/m\).

**(a) Electron accelerated through 54 V**

All the work done by the field becomes kinetic energy:

\(K = eV = (1.6 \times 10^{-19})(54) = 8.64 \times 10^{-18}\) J

\(p = \sqrt{2m_eK} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 8.64 \times 10^{-18}} = 3.968 \times 10^{-24}\) kg m/s

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{3.968 \times 10^{-24}} = 1.671 \times 10^{-10}\) m \(= 1.671\ \mathring{A} = 0.1671\) nm

\(v = \dfrac{p}{m_e} = \dfrac{3.968 \times 10^{-24}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}} = 4.355 \times 10^{6}\) m/s

As a check, the chapter's Eq. (14.7) gives \(\lambda = 1.228/\sqrt{V}\) nm \(= 1.228/\sqrt{54} = 0.1671\) nm, which agrees. (This is the wavelength used in the Davisson-Germer experiment.)

**(b) Electron with kinetic energy 150 eV**

\(K = 150 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 2.4 \times 10^{-17}\) J

\(p = \sqrt{2m_eK} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.4 \times 10^{-17}} = 6.613 \times 10^{-24}\) kg m/s

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{6.613 \times 10^{-24}} = 1.003 \times 10^{-10}\) m \(= 1.003\ \mathring{A} = 0.1003\) nm

\(v = \dfrac{p}{m_e} = \dfrac{6.613 \times 10^{-24}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}} = 7.259 \times 10^{6}\) m/s

The larger kinetic energy gives a larger momentum and hence a **shorter** wavelength, as \(\lambda \propto 1/\sqrt{K}\).

**Answer: (a) \(\lambda = 1.671\ \mathring{A}\), \(p = 3.968 \times 10^{-24}\) kg m/s, \(v = 4.355 \times 10^{6}\) m/s. (b) \(\lambda = 1.003\ \mathring{A}\), \(p = 6.613 \times 10^{-24}\) kg m/s, \(v = 7.259 \times 10^{6}\) m/s.**

**Data:** the electron and the proton have the same de Broglie wavelength, \(\lambda_e = \lambda_p = \lambda\). Take \(m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\) kg and \(m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg.

**(i) Ratio of their momenta**

The de Broglie relation is \(\lambda = h/p\), so \(p = h/\lambda\). The momentum depends on the wavelength alone — the mass does not enter. Hence

\(\dfrac{p_e}{p_p} = \dfrac{h/\lambda}{h/\lambda} = 1\)

\(\therefore\ p_e : p_p = 1 : 1\) — the two momenta are **equal**.

**(ii) Ratio of their kinetic energies**

For a non-relativistic particle, \(K = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m}\). With \(p_e = p_p\), the kinetic energy is inversely proportional to the mass:

\(\dfrac{K_e}{K_p} = \dfrac{p^{2}/2m_e}{p^{2}/2m_p} = \dfrac{m_p}{m_e}\)

\(\therefore\ \dfrac{K_e}{K_p} = \dfrac{1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}} = 1833\)

So the electron, being about 1833 times lighter, must carry about 1833 times the kinetic energy of the proton to have the same wavelength.

**Answer: (i) \(p_e : p_p = 1 : 1\) (equal momenta); (ii) \(K_e : K_p = m_p : m_e \approx 1833 : 1\).**

**Data:** two particles have the same de Broglie wavelength; the faster one moves 4 times as fast as the slower; the slower particle is an \(\alpha\)-particle, of mass \(m_\alpha \approx 4u\) (\(u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\) kg, so \(m_\alpha \approx 6.64 \times 10^{-27}\) kg).

Since \(\lambda = h/p = h/mv\), equal wavelengths mean equal **momenta**:

\(m_\alpha v_\alpha = m_x v_x\)

The unknown particle is the faster one, so \(v_x = 4v_\alpha\):

\(m_\alpha v_\alpha = m_x (4 v_\alpha)\)

\(\therefore\ m_x = \dfrac{m_\alpha}{4} = \dfrac{4u}{4} = u \approx 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\) kg

So the second particle must have a mass of about one atomic mass unit — one quarter of the \(\alpha\)-particle's mass. Being four times faster, it must be four times lighter for the momenta to match.

The particles of this mass are the **proton** and the **neutron** (each \(\approx 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg); a hydrogen atom, or a hydrogen nucleus, also fits. It cannot be an electron, which is roughly 1800 times lighter still.

**Answer: the other particle has mass \(m_x = m_\alpha/4 \approx 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg \(\approx 1u\) — that is, a proton or a neutron (equivalently a hydrogen nucleus/atom).**

**Data:** proton of de Broglie wavelength \(\lambda = 0.08\ \mathring{A} = 0.08 \times 10^{-10}\) m \(= 8 \times 10^{-12}\) m. Take \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s and \(m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg.

The de Broglie relation for a particle of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(v\) is

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{m_p v}\)

\(\therefore\ v = \dfrac{h}{m_p \lambda}\)

\(\therefore\ v = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{(1.67 \times 10^{-27})(8 \times 10^{-12})}\)

\(\therefore\ v = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{1.336 \times 10^{-38}} = 4.963 \times 10^{4}\) m/s

Check: \(p = m_p v = 8.288 \times 10^{-23}\) kg m/s, and \(h/\lambda = 8.288 \times 10^{-23}\) kg m/s — they agree.

This speed is about \(1.7 \times 10^{-4}\) times the speed of light, so the non-relativistic treatment is justified.

**Answer: \(v = 4.963 \times 10^{4}\) m/s \(\approx 4.96 \times 10^{4}\) m/s.**

**Data:** kinetic energy of the neutrons \(E = 5 \times 10^{-21}\) J (already in joule, so no conversion from eV is needed). Take \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s and the neutron mass \(m_n = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg.

**Speed**

\(E = \dfrac{1}{2}m_n v^{2}\)

\(\therefore\ v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E}{m_n}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 5 \times 10^{-21}}{1.67 \times 10^{-27}}} = \sqrt{5.988 \times 10^{6}}\)

\(\therefore\ v = 2.447 \times 10^{3}\) m/s \(= 2447\) m/s

**Wavelength**

\(p = m_n v = (1.67 \times 10^{-27})(2.447 \times 10^{3}) = 4.087 \times 10^{-24}\) kg m/s

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{4.087 \times 10^{-24}} = 1.622 \times 10^{-10}\) m

\(\therefore\ \lambda = 1.622\ \mathring{A} = 0.1622\) nm

(Equivalently \(\lambda = h/\sqrt{2m_nE}\), which gives the same value.) Note that this wavelength is comparable with the spacing between atoms in a crystal, which is precisely why such slow "thermal" neutrons are used for neutron diffraction studies of crystal structure.

**Answer: \(v = 2.447 \times 10^{3}\) m/s and \(\lambda = 1.622 \times 10^{-10}\) m \(= 1.622\ \mathring{A}\).**

**Data:** an electron (\(m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\) kg) and a proton (\(m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg), with \(\dfrac{m_p}{m_e} = 1833\).

The de Broglie wavelength is \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\), and for a non-relativistic particle \(p = mv = \sqrt{2mK}\).

**(a) Same speed \(v\)**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}\), so at a common speed \(\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{m}\):

\(\dfrac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p} = \dfrac{m_p}{m_e} = \dfrac{1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}} = 1833\)

\(\therefore\ \lambda_e : \lambda_p \approx 1833 : 1\) — the **electron** has the longer wavelength.

**(b) Same kinetic energy \(K\)**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\), so at a common energy \(\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\):

\(\dfrac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p}{m_e}} = \sqrt{1833} = 42.8\)

\(\therefore\ \lambda_e : \lambda_p \approx 42.8 : 1\) — again the **electron** has the longer wavelength, but the advantage is only the square root of the mass ratio.

**(c) Same momentum \(p\)**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\) depends on the momentum alone, and the mass does not appear:

\(\dfrac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p} = 1\)

\(\therefore\ \lambda_e : \lambda_p = 1 : 1\) — the two wavelengths are **equal**, so neither is longer.

**Answer: (a) \(\lambda_e : \lambda_p = m_p : m_e \approx 1833 : 1\), electron longer; (b) \(\lambda_e : \lambda_p = \sqrt{m_p/m_e} \approx 42.8 : 1\), electron longer; (c) \(\lambda_e : \lambda_p = 1 : 1\), equal — neither is longer.**
